analysis.one_liner: Ends real-estate tax breaks for companies that own and run private prisons.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2013, the two big private prison companies have organized as real estate investment trusts — a structure that lets them avoid most corporate income tax. The tax code already bars companies that operate lodging or health care facilities from using that structure. This bill would add prison facilities to that exclusion, so companies running correctional, detention, or penal facilities would have to pay the corporate taxes they currently avoid.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would collect corporate income tax from private prison companies that currently shelter their prison income through the real estate investment trust structure. The bill would also remove a tax incentive that rewards profitable incarceration.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the tax code so that a corporation that operates or manages a prison facility, or provides services in connection with one, can no longer count as a taxable REIT subsidiary — ending the structure private prison companies use to avoid corporate income tax.
Extends an exclusion that already applies to lodging and health care facilities to prisons, defined to cover any correctional, detention, or penal facility.

analysis.who_pays: Private prison companies and their shareholders, who would lose the real estate investment trust tax advantage and pay corporate income tax on prison-related profits. Their investors, including retirement funds holding the stock, would bear the cost through lower returns.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison companies and their investors

drawbacks.text: The real estate investment trust structure is available to any qualifying real estate company under the tax code; opponents of the structure's use by lodging and health care companies have argued it is applied selectively, and this bill extends that selectivity to one more industry rather than addressing it across the board.

The bill changes only the tax treatment of private prisons. It does not reduce incarceration, end private prison contracts, or impose operating conditions on the companies, so its practical effect on how prisons are run is indirect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — recovering corporate tax revenue from companies avoiding it through a real estate structure — is real but modest in scale, and no revenue estimate or committee analysis was ever produced because the bill received no hearing. The main cost falls on the prison companies and their shareholders. The larger limit is that the bill addresses the tax break, not the private prison industry itself.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gregory Meeks introduced the bill on November 6, 2017, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law.
Four Democratic members cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prison companies and their shareholders are better off, because they keep the real estate investment trust tax structure and the corporate tax it avoids. No member of Congress paid any price for the bill receiving no consideration.

for.name: Rep. Gregory W. Meeks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip prison operators of the REIT tax structure.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax law, chaired by Rep. Kevin Brady (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Set the House floor agenda in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with no committee action, it never reached a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters — the sponsor and four cosponsors — were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee and House never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Private prison operators (CoreCivic, GEO Group) and their REIT investors
industries.note: The companies converted to real estate investment trusts in 2013 and pay little corporate income tax on prison profits. The bill would end that advantage; its defeat preserves it. These companies' revenue comes from government contracts to house inmates, so their tax savings come at the public's expense.
The bill would amend REIT rules, but only to cover prison facilities; lodging and health care REITs already face the same exclusion, and other REITs are untouched.
